gotcha_text: Landlords leverage relocation clauses to shuffle tenants into inferior spaces to facilitate redevelopment or premium tenant placement. This leaves franchisees footing the bill for signage, remodeling, and lost foot traffic during the transition.
fix_text: Tenant Pulse identifies vague relocation language and suggests specific language for landlord-funded build-outs. Our tool flags missing reimbursement requirements for all capital expenditures associated with the move.
deep_dive_html:
The Strategic Risk of Discretionary Relocation

For franchisees, a lease is more than a right to occupy space; it is a blueprint for brand execution. Relocation clauses, often buried in the 'Miscellaneous' or 'Demolition' sections, grant landlords the unilateral power to move your operations to a different unit within the center. While landlords frame this as a necessity for property redevelopment, the economic reality is often a transfer of risk from the landlord to the tenant. An unmitigated relocation clause allows a landlord to move a high-performing franchise into a 'dead' corner or a unit with inferior visibility, effectively cannibalizing your revenue to facilitate a more lucrative tenant's entry.

The financial implications extend far beyond simple moving costs. A forced move triggers a cascade of unbudgeted capital expenditures, including:

  • Complete rebranding and signage replacement to meet strict franchise standards.
  • Structural modifications to accommodate new floor plans or utility configurations.
  • Loss of revenue during the transition period and construction downtime.
  • Potential breach of franchise agreements if the new site fails to meet specific site-selection criteria.

Negotiating Enforceable Relocation Protections

To neutralize this threat, a lease must move beyond mere 'notice' and toward 'reimbursement and comparability.' A sophisticated tenant demands that any relocation be contingent upon the landlord providing a space of equal or greater prominence, visibility, and utility. Furthermore, the clause must explicitly mandate that the landlord bears 100% of the costs associated with the move, including all construction, permitting, and rebranding expenses, as well as any loss of business income during the transition.

A robust relocation provision should also include a 'Right of Refusal,' allowing the franchisee to reject any proposed space that does not meet the pre-defined technical specifications of the brand. Without these safeguards, you are essentially granting the landlord an option to devalue your business at their whim.

title: Hidden Traps in Relocation Clauses for Franchisees
